prompt: A real spacecraft photograph of a thin crescent Earth hanging high in a flat black sky, taken handheld through a window with a digital camera at long focal length, like the Artemis II and Orion Earth frames. The attached reference image is the house's approved plate: match its real-camera finish, its fine sensor grain and its empty frame, but not its subject. The subject: Earth as a crescent about one fifth of the frame height across, placed in the upper left of the frame, its centre about a quarter of the way in from the left edge and a quarter of the way down from the top. The light: one hard, unfiltered sun from the left, so the lit crescent is on Earth's left limb and the crescent's horns point to the right. The crescent is mostly cloud: bright white and pale grey cloud decks, streets of cumulus, with only a few small patches of dull grey-blue ocean showing between them; no coastlines, no continents, no hurricane swirl, no shiny ocean highlight. The terminator is hard and rough, broken by cloud texture. Just to the right of the terminator, on the otherwise pure black night side, three or four tiny isolated bright white flecks: the tops of tall thunderstorm anvils still in sunlight after the ground below them has gone dark. Everything else on the night side is empty black, no city lights, no glow, no detail. Along the outer lit edge only, Earth's air is a single hairline of pale blue, thinner than a pencil line, ending sharply in the black, never a halo, never spreading outward. The sky: pure neutral black, unexposed, flat from corner to corner, no gradient, no colour cast, no stars at all. The lower third of the frame is completely empty pure black, nothing in it, left clear for a horizon to be added later. The finish: grainy, sharp, slightly noisy sensor grain on the lit cloud like a real raw spacecraft frame, no gloss, no CGI smoothness, true black around the body. No lens flare, no streaks, no bloom, no limb glow, no stars, no nebula, no text, no labels, no ground, no spacecraft parts.

A real black-and-white Cassini narrow-angle camera frame of Saturn hanging high in a flat black sky, monochrome greyscale through a clear filter. The attached reference image is the house's approved plate: match its real-camera finish, its fine grain and its empty frame, but not its subject. The subject: Saturn as a crescent, the whole globe about a third of the frame height across, placed in the upper right, its centre about two thirds of the way across from the left and a third of the way down from the top. The light: one hard, unfiltered sun from the left, so only the left limb of the globe is lit as a fat crescent; the right part of the globe is pure black, merging into the black sky with no outline and no rim light. The lit crescent is smooth grey with soft horizontal cloud bands in slightly different greys, a real gas-giant surface, not a CG ball. The rings are seen almost exactly edge-on: one razor-thin straight horizontal line, thinner than a hair, crossing the globe at its equator and running out past both sides of the planet into the black, pale grey on the left, faint and grey on the right. Just below the ring line on the lit crescent, the rings' shadow: a thin, sharp, dark grey stripe laid across the lit cloud bands, parallel to the ring line, hard-edged. The planet does not sit on the rings; there is no broad ring ellipse, no ring plane under it. The sky: pure neutral black, unexposed, flat from corner to corner, no gradient, no colour cast, no stars at all. The lower third of the frame is completely empty pure black, nothing in it, left clear for a horizon to be added later. The finish: grainy raw spacecraft telemetry, visible fine sensor noise on the lit crescent, slight compression texture, hard terminator, true black around the body, no gloss. No colour, no limb halo, no haze glow round the planet, no lens flare, no streaks, no bloom, no moons, no stars, no text, no labels, no arrows, no ground.

A real total solar eclipse photograph taken from space, an airless view: the Sun's corona around the black disc of the Moon, high in a flat black sky. The attached reference image is the house's approved eclipse plate: match its real-camera corona with fine streamers and its dark disc, but make the black truly black, not milky grey, and leave out any horizontal streak. The subject: the black disc of the Moon about one fifth of the frame height across, placed in the upper part of the frame a little left of centre, its centre about two fifths of the way across from the left and a third of the way down from the top. Around it the white corona: many fine, thin, straight radial streamers like combed hair, longer and fanned along the left-right axis, shorter brush-like plumes at top and bottom, pearl white fading quickly to black within about one disc width, with structure all the way in, never a smooth round glow. The disc is pure black, a hard clean edge, no detail on it. The light: the Sun is just emerging on the left limb of the disc, so on the left edge sits a short broken string of four or five tiny brilliant white beads of sunlight, separated by dark gaps where lunar mountains still block it, the beads following the curve of the limb; one or two thin pink prominences beside them. No rays from the beads, no starburst, no streak, no ring of flare. The sky: pure neutral black, unexposed, flat from corner to corner, no gradient, no colour cast, no stars at all. The corona must not reach the lower third. The lower third of the frame is completely empty pure black, nothing in it, left clear for a horizon to be added later. The finish: a real long-lens camera frame, fine grain in the corona, sharp streamer detail, true black around the corona, no gloss, no CGI. No lens flare, no horizontal or anamorphic streaks, no hexagon ghosts, no bloom beyond the corona, no Earth, no stars, no text, no labels, no ground.

A real spacecraft photograph of the Moon, small and far away, hanging high in a vast flat black sky, like the Orion frame of the Moon from distant retrograde orbit. The attached reference image is the house's approved plate: match its real-camera finish, its fine grain and its empty frame, but not its subject. The subject: the Moon at exact quarter phase, a half disc only about one eighth of the frame height across, placed in the upper part of the frame a little right of centre, its centre about three fifths of the way across from the left and a quarter of the way down from the top; all the rest of the frame is black. The light: one hard, unfiltered sun from the left, so the left half of the disc is lit and the right half is pure black and invisible against the sky. The terminator runs straight up and down through the middle of the disc, but at close look it is serrated: crater rims and mountain tops just past the line catch the low sun as tiny bright points and short bright arcs, and crater floors just inside it are filled with long hard black shadow. The lit half is dull, dark grey-brown and grey like worn asphalt, with darker smooth maria patches and bright crater rays toward the left limb; craters scattered irregularly, never arranged into a face. The left limb is a clean hard edge against black. No glow, no halo and no rim light on the Moon; it is airless. The Moon casts no shadow anywhere; the sky behind it is empty. The sky: pure neutral black, unexposed, flat from corner to corner, no gradient, no colour cast, no brightening toward the bottom, no stars at all. The lower third of the frame is completely empty pure black, nothing in it, left clear for a horizon to be added later. The finish: a grainy real spacecraft frame, fine sensor noise on the lit surface, sharp, hard terminator, true black around the body, no gloss, no CGI. No lens flare, no streaks, no bloom, no Earth, no stars, no nebula, no text, no labels, no ground.
